attributes.readMe:
## Placement Board (PB)

A plan for putting things in places — seats at tables, technicians on shifts, boxes on shelves, candidates in interview slots.

The board holds three things:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `zones` | where things **can** go (`PlacementZoneField`) |
| `placements` | the committed arrangement — what is true now |
| `draft` | what the user is proposing |
| `pool` | the candidate items (`linksToMany(CardDef)`) |

Anything in `pool` but not in `draft` shows in the palette. That is the progress signal: the rail shrinks as the plan fills, so no separate counter is needed.

### Why a draft at all

This is the distinguishing move of the family, and the reason **Commit Placement** is a separate command rather than a save button.

Dragging a person to a seat is a *proposal*. It is only real once the whole arrangement has been checked — no table over capacity, nobody double-seated, nobody left out. A board that wrote through on every drag would make the half-finished state the live one, and there is no half-finished seating plan that is safe to publish.

So the two halves pull in opposite directions on purpose:

- **the board is permissive** — an over-capacity draft is allowed to exist, because the user has to *see* the conflict to resolve it. A drag that is silently swallowed teaches nothing.
- **the commit gate is strict** — `CommitPlacementCommand` refuses while any zone is over capacity, unless overridden explicitly.

### Computed state

`placedCount`, `unplacedCount`, `hasUncommittedChanges`, `conflictCount`, `isCommittable`. All derived from `draft` vs `placements` — never stored, so they cannot drift from the arrays they describe.

`isCommittable` is deliberately `dirty && no conflicts`, which is exactly the condition the command enforces. The header badge and the command's refusal read the same predicate, so the UI can never promise a commit the command will reject.

### Item identity — the part that bites

`PlacementField.itemId` is a plain string, because the family works for things that are not cards (a seat number, an SKU, an imported row). But a card's runtime `id` is realm-absolute (`https://…/my-realm/Author/jane-doe`) while an authored instance writes the relative form (`../Author/jane-doe`).

Comparing those raw means a hand-authored board never matches its own pool and every item reads as unplaced. So every comparison goes through `itemKey()`, which normalises to the **last two path segments** — `Author/jane-doe`. That is stable across realms and survives the board being copied to staging.

The cost: two instances with the same name under the same type name collide. Acceptable here because a board's pool is a curated set the author chose, not an open query.

### Why `pool` is a `linksToMany` and not a live query

The platform's general rule is that membership should be a live query rather than a maintained link list. A placement board is the exception: its candidate set is a decision the author makes ("these 40 guests"), not a filter over everything that happens to match. A board that silently gained a row because someone else created a card would invalidate a plan that was already half made.

### Not a kanban — and where the line actually is

boxel-ui's `KanbanPlane` and the catalog's `Board` own the columns-of-cards case, including a WIP limit per column (`wipLimit`) and their own pointer-based drag engine. The overlap is real, and `KanbanPlane` even calls its item-in-column association `placements`.

Three things kanban does not have, and this family exists for:

1. **A palette.** On a kanban every card is already in some column; there is no "not yet anywhere" state to render.
2. **Staging.** A kanban drag writes immediately. Here it does not.
3. **Free-form zones.** A kanban is N vertical lists. A placement zone is positioned by the host — a seating chart, a floor plan, a shelf diagram.

**If you only need columns, WIP limits and immediate moves, use the catalog's `Board` instead.** This family earns its place on the palette and the staging, nothing else.

### Placing from the keyboard

Every drag has a menu equivalent. Each item in the palette has a menu of "Place in <zone>" entries, and each placed item has Move up, Move down, Move to <zone> and Remove. Both are Pret UI `Menu`s, so arrow keys, Enter and Escape work as they do in any menu. Moving an item keeps its placement `note`.

### Non-goals

Not a scheduler — zones have no time axis (use `Calendar` for that). Not an optimiser; it records a human's arrangement and never proposes one. Not a permissions model: who may commit is the host's question.

### Family

`placement-vocabulary` (shared fields + pure logic) · `components/placement-palette` · `components/placement-drop-zone` · `commands/commit-placement-command`.
